title: At the café — and the ending that marks the object
goal: Order food and drinks politely, and attach the *-t* ending that marks the part of the sentence receiving the action.
bekal: form the object ending *-t* on any noun
ask what's in a dish and ask for the bill

dialogs.title: Dialogue — A kávézóban
dialogs.intro: A small café near Nyugati pályaudvar. Budi is hungry, and the menu on the wall is full of words he has never seen.

lines.speaker: Pincér:
lines.id: Good afternoon! What would you like?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tejjel. És egy pohár vizet is kérek.
lines.id: With milk. And a glass of water too, please.
lines.literal: milk-with. and a glass water-OBJ also I-ask.

lines.speaker: Pincér:
lines.id: All right. Would you like something to eat as well?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Igen. Bocsánat, mi az a lángos?
lines.id: Yes. Excuse me, what is lángos?
lines.literal: yes. sorry, what that the lángos?

lines.speaker: Pincér:
lines.text: Az egy magyar étel. Sült tészta, tejföllel és sajttal.
lines.id: It's a Hungarian dish. Fried dough with sour cream and cheese.
lines.literal: that a Hungarian food. fried dough, sour-cream-with and cheese-with.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Is it good? And is it big enough?

lines.speaker: Pincér:
lines.text: Nagyon finom, és elég nagy egy embernek.
lines.id: Very good, and big enough for one person.
lines.literal: very tasty, and enough big a person-for.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Good, then I'll have a lángos.

lines.speaker: Pincér:
lines.text: Máris hozom. Tessék, egy kávé tejjel!
lines.id: Coming right up. Here you are, a coffee with milk!
lines.literal: right-away I-bring-it. here-you-are, a coffee milk-with!

notes: **The -t ending marks the object, not a place.** *Egy kávét kérek* = "I'd like a coffee". The coffee is **what is being asked for**, so it takes *-t*. English marks this role only by word order; Hungarian marks it with an ending — and that is exactly why its word order is free: *Kérek egy kávét* is just as correct.

**Kérek or kérem?** *Kérek* is used when the thing is not yet specific (*egy kávét kérek*), *kérem* when it is clear which one (*a számlát kérem* — the bill). This is your first glimpse of the two sets of verb endings covered fully in Unit 11. For now, just learn these two sentences as they are.
**Szépen makes your order friendly.** Literally "nicely". *Egy kávét kérek szépen* sounds warm without being over the top; it is the equivalent of adding "please" in English.

**Tejjel = tej + -vel.** The "with" ending is *-val/-vel*, and its *v* merges into the consonant before it, doubling that consonant: *tej* → *tej**jel***, *sajt* → *sajt**tal***, *tejföl* → *tejföl**lel***. The rule is unpacked in Unit 15; here just recognize the pattern.

**Nélkül stands on its own.** It is a *névutó* (postposition) like *mellett* from Unit 4, so the noun stays bare: *tej nélkül*, *cukor nélkül*. Notice that "with" sticks to the word but "without" does not — an asymmetric pair, and that is simply how it is.

**Mit is mi + -t.** Even question words obey the object rule: *Mi ez?* (What is this?) versus *Mit kérsz?* (What would you like?). Likewise *Ki?* → *Kit?* (who/whom, as the object). If you can't decide, ask yourself: is this word **receiving** the action? It's the same logic as English *who* vs *whom*.

grammars.title: The object ending -t
body: One letter, three situations. Notice that the third is exactly the same as the plural rule in Unit 3 — Hungarian reuses the same pattern everywhere.

head: Noun ends in
What is added
Example
rows: s, sz, r, l, n, ny

after: **The -at group to memorize.** Some back-vowel words take *-at* instead of *-ot* — and the list is exactly the same as the *-ak* plural group from Unit 3: *ház* → *házat*, *hal* → *halat*, *fal* → *falat*, *toll* → *tollat*, *út* → *utat*. If you already know *házak*, you already know *házat*.

**Some words shorten or drop a vowel.** *víz* → *vizet*, *kenyér* → *kenyeret*, *cukor* → *cukrot*, *étterem* → *éttermet*, *nyár* → *nyarat*. This happens with every ending, not just *-t*, so once you know one form, you know them all.

**When is -t used?** Whenever the noun answers the question "what receives the action": *Kérek egy kávét*, *Eszem egy lángost*, *Olvasom a könyvet*. If the noun only names a place, a time, or a tool, it does not take *-t*.

grammars.title: Kérek, szeretnék — two ways to order
body: Both are polite. The second is slightly softer, and almost always safe.

head: Magyar
Say it
Tone
Meaning
rows: Could you bring me a coffee?

after: *Szeretnék* is actually the conditional of *szeretek* ("I like") — literally "I would like". Exactly the same as English *I would like*.
To order more than one item, link them with *és* and put *-t* on **each one**: *Egy kávét és egy pohár vizet kérek.* Leaving the *-t* off the second item is the most common mistake beginners make.

grammars.title: Question words take the ending too
body: If the question word asks about the object, it also takes *-t*.

head: Not the object
As the object
Example
rows: *Kit vársz?* = Who are you waiting for?
*Melyiket kéred?* = Which one would you like?
*Mennyit kérsz?* = How much would you like?

after: Notice the word order: a Hungarian question word always stands **right before the verb**. *Mit kérsz?*, not *Kérsz mit?*. This position rule later applies to any emphasized part of the sentence as well — and that is the key to Hungarian word order, which is often called "free" but is nothing of the sort.

blocks.text: Three dishes you must try and must be able to pronounce: **gulyás** (GOO-yahsh) — the paprika beef soup that outside Hungary is called "goulash" and wrongly thought to be thick; **pörkölt** (PÖR-költ) — the one that really is thick; and **lángos** (LAHN-gohsh) — fried dough topped with sour cream and cheese, sold at markets and thermal baths.

blocks.title: Three Hungarian café habits
items: **Water doesn't come automatically.** Free tap water is rarely served unless you ask. Order *egy pohár vizet* if you want some.

**Service is around ten percent** and is often already on the bill as *szervizdíj*. If not, say the total you want to pay as you hand over the money — the local habit is to name a figure, not to leave change on the table.
**Egészségedre** is used for toasting, and the polite form is *Egészségére*. The word looks long and scary at first, but it becomes one of the most enjoyable to say once your tongue gets used to it.
